dotenv and Fail-Fast Validation

Loading .env into process.env, and checking it once at startup instead of trusting it blindly.

Node doesn't read a .env file on its own — process.env only ever contains variables the operating system actually set. The dotenv package bridges that gap: it reads a .env file and copies its contents into process.env, so the rest of the app can use it as if the OS had set those variables itself.

# .env
PORT=3000

.env is never committed to git (see .gitignore) since it's where real secrets (a database password, an API key) will live from Week 2 onward — each developer keeps their own copy locally. .env.example is committed, holding the same keys with placeholder/default values, so a new clone of the project shows you exactly what config it needs without exposing anyone's real values.

Figure 1.13 is where this project loads and checks it:

// Figure 1.13: loading and validating config (src/config/env.js)
import 'dotenv/config';

const port = Number(process.env.PORT);

if (!process.env.PORT || Number.isNaN(port)) {
  throw new Error('Missing or invalid PORT in .env — expected a number');
}

export default { PORT: port };

import 'dotenv/config' is an import kept purely for its side effect — notice nothing is assigned from it. Just importing it is what loads .env into process.env, before anything else in the file runs.

The if check is the important habit: fail fast, at startup, with a clear message — one plain manual check, the same style as the validation already in ticket.controller.js (a schema-based version arrives with Zod in Week 3). Without it, a missing or malformed PORT wouldn't crash here; it would surface later as app.listen(NaN, ...) silently picking a random port, or some far more confusing failure — the kind of bug that costs an hour to trace back to one typo in a .env file. Throwing immediately, with a message that names the actual problem, is far cheaper.
